Thank you for joining the UiPath Agentic Automation Workshop!

This handbook is your practical guide for the hands-on exercise. It walks you through each step, explains what's happening and why, and helps you build something real by the end of the session.

docs.title: What You'll Build
docs.text:
You'll implement a Benefit Claims process from the government sector — the procedure citizens use to request financial or service-based assistance, such as pensions, social assistance, or unemployment benefits.

Along the way you'll bring together most of the platform. You'll model the end-to-end process as a BPMN diagram, orchestrate it in Maestro, extract data from a claim PDF with IXP and an RPA workflow, build three AI agents that verify residency, verify income, and determine eligibility, add a human validation step so a case worker makes the final call, and wire up Integration Service to notify the applicant either way.

That's nine steps, each building on the last. By the end you'll have one process that coordinates robots, agents, and a human — which is what agentic orchestration actually looks like in production.

Congratulations!

You've completed the Agentic Automation Workshop — from your first CLI command to a live, running Benefit Claims process built with Maestro, IXP, three AI agents, and a coding agent.

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
Across this workshop you set up your coding agent environment, practiced driving the platform from the terminal, and used both hands-on clicking and a coding agent to build an end-to-end Benefit Claims Processing solution — an agentic process that verifies a citizen's benefits application and routes it to a human for the final call.

docs.title: 1. Keep building with a coding agent
docs.text: If you built the Income Verification Agent manually, go back and try the coding agent path — or pick another agent in the process and rebuild it the other way. The fastest way to get comfortable is to keep switching between describing outcomes to your coding agent and configuring things by hand, until reaching for the CLI feels as natural as clicking through Studio Web.

docs.title: 2. Extend the process
docs.text: Nothing about this process is final. Add a guardrail to one of the agents, tighten a prompt after watching it misfire on an edge case, or add a fourth verification check of your own. Small, incremental changes are the fastest way to build intuition for how these agents actually behave.

docs.title: Keep iterating
docs.text:
Ask for outcomes, not commands

  • Describe what you want the agent to do and let it choose the uip commands. It gets easier the more you do it.

Evaluate before you trust

  • Before relying on any agent's decision in production, build out its evaluation set. A few good test cases catch more regressions than hours of manual testing.

Trust the model

  • Don't over-optimize for tokens early. A stronger model often costs less overall because it makes fewer mistakes.

docs.title: Benefit Claims Processing
docs.text: Build an end-to-end agentic Benefit Claims process — BPMN modelling, IXP document extraction, three AI agents, human validation, and email notification.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Agentic orchestration, implemented in Maestro, lets you coordinate long-running enterprise processes between humans, robots, and AI agents working across different systems of record and systems of engagement. You design, implement, monitor, operate, and optimize those processes, then run them at scale.

In this exercise you'll implement a Benefit Claims use case from the government sector — the structured procedure citizens use to request financial or service-based assistance, such as pensions, social assistance, or unemployment benefits.

docs.title: Automating Business Processes using BPMN canvas
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this lesson:

  1. Review the Benefit Claims process and its six common steps
  2. Open the BPMN designer and import the Benefit Claims diagram
  3. Analyze the diagram and map each process step onto it

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Modeling starts with process diagramming and optimization. Before building anything, you'll review the process you're about to implement and see it drawn as a BPMN diagram — the shape the rest of the exercise fills in.

docs.title: Let's draft a simple process
docs.text:
Let's practice agentic automation using a simplified version of the Benefit Claims process.

Here are the common steps of the Benefit Claims process we are going to implement:

  1. Application Submitted — Applicant submits a completed benefits application, along with any other required documents, like proof of income, proof of residency, proof of identity, etc.
  2. Application processing — The benefits application is processed and checked for completeness. If any information is missing, the applicant is contacted.
  3. Fraud checks — fraud checks are being conducted by AI Agents to verify:
    1. The residency address declared by the applicant corresponds with the address from existing records.
    2. The income amount declared by the applicant corresponds with existing records.
  4. Eligibility determination — Based on the declared household size and monthly income, the benefit guidelines are checked by an AI Agent to determine whether the applicant qualifies for benefits or not. This is the step where the benefit amount is also being calculated.
  5. Case Worker Review — The case worker is presented with the complete case information: application information, fraud check results and eligibility determination made by the agents. The worker makes a decision whether to Approve or Deny the benefits claim.
  6. Application Notification — The applicant is informed about the decision made by the case worker.

It allows users to create visual flowcharts — including start/end events, tasks, and gateways — that can be directly converted into automated workflows within UiPath Maestro.

docs.title: Build the Benefit Claims Assistant (Conversational Agent)
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this lesson:

  1. Build a conversational AI Agent in Studio Web that answers questions about the benefits program, using the Eligibility context
  2. Let the same agent register new applications: collect the documents in the chat, upload them and start the Benefit Claims Processing workflow
  3. Test both scenarios in the agent's chat

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: By the end of this lesson you'll have a Benefits Assistant that applicants can chat with. It answers questions about the SNAP program from the official documents, and it registers a new application end to end: it asks for the applicant's email, then the application, then the paystub, stores both files and starts the existing Benefit Claims Processing workflow, without waiting for the decision.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
The agent has two jobs:

  • Job A: answer questions about the SNAP benefits program, using only the official program documents in the Eligibility index.
  • Job B: register a new application. It collects the applicant's email address, then the application, then the paystub, uploads each file, and starts the existing Benefit Claims Processing workflow.
                        Applicant (chat window)
                                  |
                                  v
              +-----------------------------------------+
              | Benefits Assistant Conversational Agent |
              +-----------------------------------------+
                 |                 |                  |
     Job A       |       Job B     |                  |   Job B (after "yes")
                 v                 v                  v
        +--------------+  +---------------------+  +----------------------+
        | Eligibility  |  | UploadFileTo        |  | Start Benefit Claim  |
        | index (RAG)  |  | StorageBucket  (x2) |  | (robot, no waiting)  |
        +--------------+  +---------------------+  +----------------------+
                                   |                          |
                                   v                          v
                        "Input Documents" bucket   BenefitClaimsProcessing (BPMN)
                        application + paystub      agents, case worker review,
                                                   approval / rejection email
Piece Type What it does Why it is there Benefits Assistant Conversational Agent Low-code agent, Conversational Chats with the applicant, answers questions, runs the registration flow One friendly front door for applicants Eligibility Context Grounding index (already in the solution) Returns the most relevant passages from the program documents The agent answers from official rules, not from its own memory UploadFileToStorageBucket RPA robot (already in the template) Saves a file the user attached in the chat into the Input Documents bucket and returns the real file name The BPMN reads its input files from that bucket. A robot with a file argument also lets the chat accept file uploads Start Benefit Claim RPA robot (already in the template) Starts the BenefitClaimsProcessing process with the two file names and the email, then returns right away No Integration Service connector needed. It does not wait, because the BPMN can run for days BenefitClaimsProcessing BPMN agentic process (already in the solution) Extracts data, runs the verification agents, sends the case to a case worker, emails the result Unchanged. The chat simply becomes a new way to start it

Key idea

The agent decides what to do and when. Robots do the parts that must be exact: storing files, stamping the real time, starting a process. An LLM has no reliable clock and should never guess a timestamp.

docs.title: Conversational vs. autonomous agents
docs.text:
An autonomous agent, like the ones you built in the earlier lessons, takes one input and returns one structured output. A conversational agent talks with a person over many turns, streams its replies and can ask follow-up questions. Registration needs exactly that.

That's also why a conversational agent looks different:

  • No output arguments. A conversational agent's "output" is the chat itself: its messages and the tool calls it makes. Nothing would ever fill an output schema, so leave it empty.
  • The user prompt stays blank. In an autonomous agent, the user prompt turns input arguments into a task. Here, each chat message from the user is the input. The platform sends the whole conversation to the agent on every turn.

You also don't add any input argument for "message" or "chat history". The platform provides the conversation automatically.

docs.title: 1. Create the conversational agent
docs.text:
1. In the Explorer, click Add (+) and choose Agent under Building Blocks.

  2. Name the agent:

    Benefits Assistant Conversational Agent

  3. In the Select agent type dialog, choose Conversational under LOW-CODE and click Start fresh.

  4. In the agent settings, choose the model anthropic.claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Sonnet 5).

The agent now appears in the Explorer, its type is Conversational, and it has no input or output arguments.

docs.title: 2. Add the Eligibility context
docs.text:
Context Grounding is a component of the UiPath AI Trust Layer which allows you to bring in your data to generate more accurate, reliable GenAI predictions. It stores your documents in an index: a searchable copy that returns the passages that best match a question.

The index contains the program documents (eligibility criteria and benefit calculation rules). With it, the agent answers from the official text and can show where the answer came from. Without it, the agent would answer from general knowledge, which may be outdated or simply wrong for this program.

  1. In the agent, click Add Context.

  2. Select Context Grounding Indexes.

  3. Select the Eligibility index from the current solution.

  4. Choose the Semantic search strategy.

  5. Paste this as the context description:

    SNAP program eligibility rules: income limits, deductions, household size rules and benefit amounts.

  6. Keep the search query dynamic (the agent writes the query) and paste this as the query description:

    A focused natural-language question about SNAP eligibility rules, income limits, deductions or benefit amounts.

docs.title: 3. Add the UploadFileToStorageBucket tool
docs.text:
This robot stores each attached file in the Input Documents bucket. It also has a file argument (In_File): a tool that can process files is what enables file uploads in the chat. Without it, users can't attach files.

  1. In the tools section, click +.

  2. Search for UploadFileToStorageBucket under RPA workflows and select it.

  3. Paste this into the tool Description. It tells the agent what the tool does and when to call it. The details of each value go in the argument descriptions, in the next step.

    Uploads ONE file the user attached in the chat to the 'Input Documents' storage bucket and returns the exact name it was stored under. Call it once per document, one at a time: first for the application, then, after the user has attached it, for the paystub.

  4. Fill in the argument descriptions (the text the agent reads to decide what to pass):

    • In_File:

      The single file the user attached for the current document: the application (PDF) or the paystub (PDF or PNG)

    • in_emailAddress:

      Applicant email address, exactly as provided by the user

    • in_FileName:

      Target file name: <sanitized email>_<application|paystub>_{timestamp}.<pdf|png>. Sanitized email = the email with every '@' and '.' replaced by '_'. Keep the literal text {timestamp}, the robot replaces it. The application is always .pdf; the paystub extension must match the attached file. Example: jane_doe_example_com_paystub_{timestamp}.png

docs.title: 4. Add the Start Benefit Claim tool
docs.text:
Let's add the tool that triggers the Maestro process for claim submission.

  1. In the tools section, click +.

  2. Search for Start Benefit Claim and select it.

  3. Paste this into the tool Description:

    Registers and starts a new SNAP benefit claim by launching the Benefit Claims Processing workflow in the background. Call it only once per application, after both documents are uploaded and the user has explicitly confirmed the summary. It does not return an eligibility outcome.

  4. Fill in the argument descriptions:

    • in_Application:

      The out_FileName returned by UploadFileToStorageBucket for the application PDF, exactly as returned

    • in_ExamplePaystub:

      The out_FileName returned by UploadFileToStorageBucket for the paystub (PDF or PNG), exactly as returned

    • in_emailAddress:

      Applicant email address, the same one used for the uploads

docs.title: 5. Write the System Prompt
docs.text:
The system prompt is the agent's job description. It sets the scope, the two jobs, the exact registration steps and the rules for tools. A vague prompt is the most common reason an agent misbehaves.

The prompt covers:

  • Job A, answer program questions: only from the Eligibility context; at most 3 searches per question; if the documents don't contain the answer, say so; never decide whether a specific person is eligible or estimate their benefit (that's the case worker's job, through the BPMN).
  • Job B, register an application, one file at a time:
    1. Ask for the email address.
    2. Ask for the application (PDF, max 5 MB), upload it as <sanitized email>_application_{timestamp}.pdf, and confirm it was received.
    3. Only then ask for the paystub (PDF or PNG, max 5 MB) and upload it as <sanitized email>_paystub_{timestamp}.pdf or .png, matching the file.
    4. If the user attaches two files at once, ask them to send one at a time, starting with the application.
    5. Summarise (email + the two stored file names) and ask for confirmation.
    6. Call Start Benefit Claim with the two returned out_FileName values and the email.
    7. Tell the user the application was submitted and they'll be contacted by email.

The "sanitized email" replaces every @ and . with _. Example: for jane.doe@example.com the agent sends jane_doe_example_com_application_{timestamp}.pdf, and the robot stores it as, for example, jane_doe_example_com_application_20261016143005.pdf.

Open the agent, select the System prompt field and paste the prompt below. Leave the User prompt empty.

You are the Benefits Assistant for the SNAP benefits program. You help members of the public understand the program rules and register a new benefit application. Tone: friendly, patient, clear and concise. Use plain language and avoid jargon.

Scope:
- In scope (Job A): questions about SNAP eligibility rules, deductions, income limits, household size rules and benefit amounts.
- In scope (Job B): registering a new benefit application by collecting the applicant's email, then the application (PDF), then the paystub (PDF or PNG), one at a time, and submitting the claim.
- Out of scope: any other topic, legal or tax advice, the status or outcome of an existing claim, and changes to a submitted claim. Politely say you cannot help with that and, where relevant, point the user to the benefits office.

Conversation behavior:
- On the first turn, greet the user briefly and explain that you can answer questions about SNAP eligibility rules or help them submit a new application.
- If the user's intent is unclear, ask one short clarifying question before acting.
- Handle one job at a time. If the user switches from questions to applying (or back), follow the new request.

Job A: answering eligibility questions
- Answer ONLY from information retrieved from the Eligibility context. Do not use outside knowledge about SNAP or other programs.
- Search the Eligibility context with a focused query. Search at most 3 times per user question. After the third search, stop searching and answer with what you already have.
- If the retrieved content does not cover the question, or only covers part of it, say so clearly and do not guess.
- Explain rules in general terms. Never make an eligibility decision for a specific person, never say that someone qualifies or does not qualify, and never promise or estimate a benefit amount for a specific person or household. If the user asks whether they personally qualify or how much they will get, explain the relevant general rules and invite them to submit an application so the program can assess their case.

Job B: registering a new application
Follow these steps in order. Do not skip steps.
1. Ask for the applicant's email address. If the value does not look like a valid email address, ask again.
2. Collect and upload the application first. Ask the user to attach ONLY the completed application form (a PDF file, at most 5 MB) and wait for it. Treat the file attached in reply to this request as the application. If it is missing, is not a PDF, or is larger than 5 MB, explain the problem and ask for a correct file. Then upload it with the UploadFileToStorageBucket tool: In_File = the attached application, in_emailAddress = the email address, in_FileName = <sanitized email>_application_{timestamp}.pdf. Keep the returned out_FileName and tell the user the application was received.
3. Then collect and upload the paystub. Only after the application upload has succeeded, ask the user to attach ONLY a recent paystub (a PDF or a PNG image, at most 5 MB) and wait for it. Treat the file attached in reply to this request as the paystub. If it is missing, has another format, or is larger than 5 MB, explain the problem and ask for a correct file. Then upload it with the UploadFileToStorageBucket tool: In_File = the attached paystub, in_emailAddress = the email address, in_FileName = <sanitized email>_paystub_{timestamp}.pdf for a PDF, or <sanitized email>_paystub_{timestamp}.png for a PNG. The extension must match the attached file. Keep the returned out_FileName.
   Rules for both uploads:
   - Build the sanitized email by replacing every "@" and every "." in the email address with "_". Example: jane.doe@example.com becomes jane_doe_example_com.
   - Write the text {timestamp} literally, including the curly braces. The tool replaces it with the real timestamp.
   - Ask for one file at a time. If the user attaches more than one file in a single message, do not guess which is which: ask them to send the files one at a time, starting with the application.
   - If an upload fails, tell the user and offer to try again; do not continue to step 4 until both uploads have succeeded.
4. Show a short summary: the email address and the two file names returned by the tool (application and paystub). Ask the user to confirm that the details are correct and that they want to submit the application.
5. Only after the user explicitly confirms, call the Start Benefit Claim tool once with in_Application = the out_FileName returned for the application, in_ExamplePaystub = the out_FileName returned for the paystub, and in_emailAddress = the email address. If the user does not confirm, ask what they want to change.
6. Tell the user that the application has been submitted and that they will be contacted by email about the next steps. Do not wait for the processing result, and do not guess or predict the outcome.

Tools:
- Eligibility context: use only for Job A questions, at most 3 searches per question.
- UploadFileToStorageBucket: call only in Job B steps 2 and 3, once per document, and only with a file the user attached in this conversation.
- Start Benefit Claim: call only in Job B step 5, after explicit user confirmation, and only once per application.
- Never invent, edit or reformat file names. Only pass out_FileName values exactly as returned by UploadFileToStorageBucket.

Privacy:
- Ask only for the information needed: the applicant's email and the two documents. Do not ask for social security numbers, bank details or other personal data.
- Do not repeat the contents of the uploaded documents back to the user.

Response style:
- Default to 2 to 4 sentences. Use short bullet lists for multi-part rules or summaries.
- Be warm and encouraging, but factual.

Uncertainty:
- If the Eligibility context does not cover something, say that you do not have that information and suggest contacting the benefits office.
- If a tool returns an error or an unexpected result, explain it simply and offer to retry. Never pretend that an action succeeded.

docs.title: 6. Test the agent: ask a question
docs.text:
Conversational agents are tested in the chat in Studio Web. Tool calls during the test are real: files really land in the bucket and the BPMN really starts.

Open the agent and start its test chat (Debug).

Then type:

What's the gross monthly income limit for a household of 4?

In the details of the run you see a search in the Eligibility context and no tool calls.

Try a question the documents can't answer, for example "What's the weather tomorrow?", or a specific one like "Am I eligible? I earn $3,000." The agent should say it can't help with the first one. For the second, it should explain the general rules and invite you to submit an application, without saying whether you qualify.

docs.title: 7. Test the agent: register an application
docs.text:
1. Type:

    I'd like to apply for SNAP benefits.

  2. When the agent asks, give your own email address. You'll receive the final decision email there.

  3. The agent asks for the application. Use the attach (paperclip) button in the chat and send Sample application.pdf.
  4. The agent uploads it and tells you the application was received. Then it asks for the paystub.
  5. Attach your paystub (for example Sample pay stub.png).
  6. Read the summary. It should show your email and two file names.
  7. Answer yes.

In the chat you should see:

  • The agent calls UploadFileToStorageBucket twice, in two separate turns: first for the application, then for the paystub.
  • The summary shows two different names, with a real timestamp, and the paystub keeps its own extension, for example:
    • jane_doe_example_com_application_20261016143005.pdf
    • jane_doe_example_com_paystub_20261016143112.png
  • After your confirmation, the agent calls Start Benefit Claim once.
  • The agent tells you the application was submitted and that you'll be contacted by email. It does not wait for a decision.

In Orchestrator (in the folder your debug run uses; ask your trainer if you're not sure which one):

Where What you should see Storage Buckets → Input Documents The two new files, with the names from the summary Jobs Two UploadFileToStorageBucket jobs and one Start Benefit Claim job, all Successful within seconds Jobs One BenefitClaimsProcessing job, Running Maestro → process instances The new BenefitClaimsProcessing instance with in_Application, in_ExamplePaystub and in_emailAddress filled with your values

Later, after the case worker review, the approval or rejection email arrives in your inbox.

Time to move to the next one!

docs.title: Publish the Solution
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this lesson:

  1. Deploy the Benefit Claims Processing solution from Studio Web to your personal workspace
  2. Run the process end to end

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Until now, everything ran in Debug mode inside Studio Web. In this lesson you'll publish the Benefit Claims Processing solution and deploy it, so the process, the agents, the robots and the Action App run as a real automation in Orchestrator, outside the designer.

docs.title: Publish vs. deploy
docs.text:
A UiPath Solution goes through three stages on its way to production:

Stage What happens Where Publish Studio Web packs all the projects of the solution into one versioned solution package Studio Web, then the tenant's Solutions list Deploy The package is installed into an Orchestrator folder. You choose the folder and map the resources (connections, storage buckets, indexes) Orchestrator → Solutions Activate The deployed processes, agents and apps become available and can start running Orchestrator → Solutions

Each time you publish, you get a new version of the package. You can then upgrade an existing deployment to that version, instead of deploying from scratch.

docs.title: 1. Check the solution for errors
docs.text:
Studio Web only publishes a solution when all its projects are valid.

  1. Open your Benefit Claims Processing - <Your Name> solution in Studio Web.
  2. Check the Explorer and the Problems panel for errors or warnings in any project.
  3. Fix any errors before you continue.

docs.title: 2. Deploy the solution
docs.text:
1. In the Studio Web toolbar, click Deploy.

  2. Choose the deployment destination Personal and click Deploy.

    • Personal packs and deploys the solution into your own personal workspace. Only you can see and run it, which is all you need for this exercise.
    • Shared publishes the package to a shared feed (the tenant feed or a folder feed) and deploys it into a shared Orchestrator folder, where other users with access to that folder can run it. It requires permissions to create solution folders and deployments in the tenant.

docs.title: 3. Run the process end to end
docs.text:
Now register a real application through the deployed Benefits Assistant Conversational Agent and follow it through the whole process.

  1. In Automation Cloud, go to Agents → Conversational.

  2. Find the Benefits Assistant Conversational Agent and click Open, then Chat.

  3. Register a new application, the same way you did in lesson 10:

    • type I'd like to apply for SNAP benefits.
    • give your own email address, so you receive the final email
    • attach Sample application.pdf when the agent asks for the application
    • attach Sample pay stub.png when it asks for the paystub
    • check the summary and answer yes

  4. Wait until the agent confirms that the application was submitted.

  5. Open Maestro and find the new BenefitClaimsProcessing instance. Follow it through the robot and the three agents, until it stops at the Case Worker Review task.

  6. Open the Case Worker Review task in Action Center, review the agents' conclusions, and approve or reject the application.

  7. Check your inbox for the approval or rejection email.

docs.title: Setting up the Solution
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this lesson:

  1. Create a Maestro Agentic Process Solution in Studio Web, starting from a template
  2. Connect the storage bucket that holds the applicants' files

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Create the Benefit Claims Processing solution from a prepared template, then connect the Orchestrator storage bucket the agentic process needs later.

Check your tenant first

Make sure the AgenticWorkshop tenant is selected from the top right corner.

docs.title: 1. Create an Agentic Process solution
docs.text:
Let's start by creating a new Agentic Process from a previously created template.

In the Studio Web home page go to Templates and select the Benefit Claims Processing Template_Professional. This will create a new solution, based on a project that was previously submitted as a template.

You will notice that this will create a new UiPath Solution.

A solution bundles together multiple components (processes, assets, queues, etc.) developed on the UiPath platform that work together to automate a business use case. In the UiPath context, a solution can be as simple as a Studio workflow/process, or as complex as a combination of multiple workflows or processes, agents, apps, assets, queues, storage buckets, Data service entities, etc.

Our Benefit Claims solution contains a few components:

  • The Agentic Process (Benefit Claims Processing)
  • Process Benefits Application — an RPA Workflow that uses UiPath IXP — Unstructured Documents to extract data from the Benefits Claim application.
  • Addition Tool, Multiplication Tool, Subtraction Tool — a few API workflows which will be used as tools by AI Agents
  • DownloadFileFromStorageBucket and UploadFileToStorageBucket — two RPA workflows which will help with handling files from Orchestrator Storage Buckets.
  • Start Benefit Claim — an RPA workflow that starts the Benefit Claims Processing agentic process. It will be used as a tool by a conversational agent.
  • A UiPath App, used to present claim details and decisions to Case Workers (Action App).
Learn more about the Unstructured and Complex Documents feature of IXP

The Unstructured and complex documents capability enhances the capability to handle complex unstructured documents, and uses generative AI to map fields and field groups as defined in the extraction schema and predict them with confidence and accuracy. This advanced feature is adept at extracting data from intricate elements like complex tables, charts, or graphs, and it structures the output effectively.

The process involves:

  • Reviewing initial model predictions.
  • Modifying prompt instructions iteratively based on review outcomes.
  • Annotating documents to gather ground truth for validation and to inform refining the performance of data extraction.

Extracting data from unstructured documents, such as contracts, long invoices, or other similar documents, requires a systematic and intelligent approach due to the variations in format, language, and layout.

docs.title: Goal

You'll wire that workflow into the Maestro diagram, then configure the gateway that decides whether extraction was complete.

docs.title: Automating Tasks using Robots
docs.text:
In our scenario, the agentic process receives as an input a PDF document representing the benefit claims application. This document is stored inside an Orchestrator Storage Bucket.

Let's assume that there is an external application from which the applicant uploads the application and any other supporting documents, and they get stored in the storage buckets. The start point of our agentic process are the documents from the storage bucket.

The first step in our agentic process is going to be executed using an RPA workflow and does the following tasks:

  • Download the application document from the Storage Bucket
  • Uses IXP — Unstructured Documents to extract key data points from the benefits application using Generative AI.

docs.title: IXP — Unstructured Docs
docs.text:
UiPath IXP — Unstructured Documents uses Generative Extraction to process complex, unstructured documents.

This capability is ideal for advanced document processing when:

  • documents contain paragraphs of free-form text or complex elements, such as: Complex tables, Graphics, Charts, Checkboxes, Call-out boxes, Signatures, Handwriting etc.
  • you need to extract inferred values (information that is not stated directly in the document but must be derived from context)

The general steps of the creation and deployment process within the Unstructured and complex document capability are the following:

  1. Model building
    • Upload sample documents
    • Define the document taxonomy — specific data points (fields) and their relationship (field groups) you wish to extract.
    • Build the taxonomy — configure the extraction schema and provide instructions to inform extraction predictions
    • Review LLM predictions — assess the initial predictions to gauge model performance
    • Modify prompts — adjust prompt instructions based on performance reviews and test their impact
    • Validate extractions — confirm or correct extractions to collect accurate ground truth data for further validation
  2. Model validation
    • Review performance — Review the performance statistics for each model version
    • Compare models — Evaluate different model versions
    • Refine performance
  3. Model deployment
    • Publish models — once the models achieve the desired performance level, publish and deploy models to make them available for Studio workflows
    • Roll back to a previous model version, if necessary.

docs.text: Compare the benefits applicant's declared residency address with the address from internal records. LLMs are ideal for this job — because the formatting of the two addresses can be different but still point to the same location. LLMs can be instructed to treat such scenarios accordingly.

docs.title: Configuring the input/output schemas
docs.text:
Next we are going to create the input and output arguments of the Agent. Let's understand what we are going to use the arguments for:

Agent arguments let your agent take in information about a business case and return a result, just as you might have activities or processes do. This can allow you to pass information from a trigger in Orchestrator or use the output of an agent to launch another automation.

Name Type Description declared_applicant_address String Applicant's full declared address (street, city, state, ZIP) SSN String Applicant's social security number (SSN)

Output arguments:

Name Type Description ResidencyValidationDecision String Final decision on the residency verification rationale String Explanation of why the decision was made, including any mismatches between addresses

docs.title: Context Grounding
docs.text:
Context Grounding is a component of the UiPath AI Trust Layer which allows you to bring in your data to generate more accurate, reliable GenAI predictions. Context Grounding is designed to make your business data LLM-ready without the need for any additional subscription to embedding models, vector databases, or large language models (LLMs).

You can create representative indexes and embeddings of business data that UiPath GenAI features can reference for contextual evidence at runtime. An index is a searchable copy of your documents: when the agent asks a question, it gets back the passages that match best.

In this case, we are going to use context grounding to provide the agent with residency records to match with the applicant's declared residency address.

Our residency records index contains a txt file with the information structured in a JSON format, so we are going to use the Semantic context grounding search strategy.

We are going to use the index named Residency Verification (which is already created).

docs.title: Configuring Agent's Prompts
docs.text:
Precision in prompts, like in coding, leads to powerful and predictable results. If your prompt is messy, expect messy output. Treat it like code, and write every word with purpose!

— another advice from gpt-4o

First, let's understand the difference between System prompt and User prompt.

System Prompts provide consistent guidelines that define an agent's role and capabilities, while User Prompts direct its attention to specific tasks and input parameters. Understanding this distinction is essential for effectively designing and implementing AI agents that can perform complex tasks while maintaining appropriate operational boundaries.

  • System prompt — allows you to describe in natural language the agent's role, goal and constraints. You specify any rules for it to follow, and information about when it might want to use certain tools, escalations, or context – all of which we'll cover later in this guide.
  • User prompt — User prompts allow you to structure how the inputs/arguments are passed to the agent, and you can also show in the user prompt how we'll refer to certain inputs in the system prompt.

docs.title: 5. Write the System Prompt
docs.text:
Let's start with the System Prompt. Copy the following and paste it into your System Prompt:

You are a residency verification assistant designed to verify that an applicant's provided address matches the address in our known records. Your primary goal is to determine if the application can proceed or if additional proof of residency is required.

##Instructions##
1. Search for the applicant's address in the Residency Verification index. Applicant's SSN should match the input SSN.
- If the address fully matches (Address, City, State, ZIP), set ##ResidencyValidationDecision## value as "Valid"
- If one or more address fields do not match (Address, City, State, ZIP), set ##ResidencyValidationDecision## value as "Invalid"
- If multiple addresses are found for the same SSN, try to match each one of them with the declared address and return "Valid" if one of them is a match. **DO NOT** mix and match address fields from one record to another. All fields should match from one record.
- If the applicant's address can't be found based on the SSN, set ##ResidencyValidationDecision## value as "Invalid"
- In the ##rationale## output field provide an explanation for your decision

##Matching rules##
- Ignore trailing spaces and any other formatting differences. The Address, City, State, Zip should still be considered a match if they point to the same location but formatting is different.
Always maintain a professional and impartial tone in your evaluations. Your assessments should be based solely on the address comparisons, without referencing external databases or services.

docs.title: 6. Write the User Prompt
docs.text:
User Prompt connects it all together. In our case, the user prompt looks like this — paste it into your User Prompt:

Please evaluate the residency verification for the following applicant:
Applicant Address: {{input.declared_applicant_address}}
SSN: {{input.SSN}}

docs.title: Quality Control and Evaluations
docs.text:
How about giving our agent a thorough testing?

  • Imagine that tomorrow a brand new model is released, or for some reason, for example cost, you would like to switch to an alternative LLM. How would you ensure that this change will not disrupt agent's result?
  • What if during numerous improvements and fine tuning of prompt previous document samples do not work anymore?

The solution is in automated testing, just like we do with Robots, or pretty much any other source code. Let's build Evaluations that help us with automatic validation of results for a set of predefined samples.

An evaluation is a pair between an input and an assertion — or evaluator — made on the output. The evaluator is a defined condition or rule used to assess whether the agent's output meets the expected output or expected trajectory.

There are three main categories of evaluators:

LLM-as-a-Judge:

  • Recommended as the default approach when targeting the root output.
  • Provides flexible evaluation of complex outputs.
  • Best used when evaluating reasoning, natural language responses, or complex structured outputs.

Deterministic

  • Recommended when expecting exact matches.
  • Most effective when output requirements are strictly defined
  • Works with complex objects, but is best used with:
    • Boolean responses (true/false)
    • Specific numerical values
    • Exact string matches
    • Array of primitives

Trajectory

  • Used to judge the agent's overall behavior based on its run history and expected behavior.

Our Agent has the following output fields:

  • ResidencyValidationDecision — "Valid" or "Invalid" — deterministic output
  • rationale — Explanation of why the decision was made, including any mismatches between addresses — dynamic output

Let's assume we want to test the ResidencyValidationDecision field. To do that, we will use a deterministic evaluator.

docs.title: Build the Income Verification Agent
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this lesson:

  1. Configure an RPA workflow to download the necessary documents
  2. Build the Income Verification AI Agent from scratch as a low-code agent, with Claude Code and the uipath-agents skill
    • Agent will use the applicant's paystub document to extract the applicant's Name, Social Security Number (SSN) and the monthly income
    • Based on that, the agent will use a tool to extract income information from internal records (a Data Fabric entity)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Compare the benefits applicant's monthly income against our existing records. The agent decides:

  • If the paystub income matches the existing records income, the decision is valid
  • If there is any discrepancy, the decision is invalid
  • If the paystub or existing records data is missing, the decision is invalid

LLMs are ideal for this job — because the formatting of the two input paystubs can be different but still contain the necessary information. LLMs can be instructed to treat such scenarios accordingly.

docs.text:
In our scenario, the agent receives as an input a paystub document containing the benefits applicant's details and monthly income. This document is stored inside an Orchestrator Storage Bucket.

We need to download this document and pass it as a variable to our agent. To do that, we will use an RPA workflow.

Our RPA workflow is already part of the solution and is called DownloadFileFromStorageBucket. Get familiar with it by taking a look inside. It will receive a storage bucket filepath as input and will output the file as a variable.

docs.title: Describe the Agent
docs.text:
Give your coding agent a plain-English description of what to build:

Build a low-code UiPath agent named "Income Verification Agent" that verifies an applicant's income for benefits eligibility.

It takes a paystub PDF as input. First, runs it through Analyze Files to extract the applicant's name, monthly income, and SSN (SSN is listed under "Employee ID"). If the paystub doesn't state a monthly income directly, deduce it from what it does show: gross pay for the pay period times the number of pay periods per year, divided by 12 (weekly = 52, bi-weekly = 26, semi-monthly = 24, monthly = 12), an annual salary divided by 12, or an hourly rate times the hours worked, scaled to a month. Use the pay frequency or the pay period dates on the paystub to tell which applies, and round the result to 2 decimals. Then call the existing "Retrieve Income Information" RPA process (already existent in the studio web solution) to get their income on record — just connect it as a tool, don't rebuild it.

Compare the two incomes: exact match = "valid", mismatch = "invalid". If the monthly income can't be determined from the paystub, or anything else is missing or zero, treat it as "invalid" instead of erroring. When the monthly income was deduced, explain in the rationale how it was calculated.

Output should be: { "out_decision": "valid | invalid", "out_rationale": "..." }

Don't expose the full SSN anywhere in the output, and don't guess at data that isn't actually in the paystub or the lookup result. Calculating the monthly income from figures on the paystub is fine; making up figures isn't.

At the end, upload the agent into the existing solution in UiPath Studio Web at the following URL: {URL of the project from Studio Web}

This is just an example, to show what that URL looks like — yours will be different

https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs/studio_/designer/0add336b-c1dc-4447-a2f2-b03e8169a4ef?solutionId=301d473d-e34b-47c4-90a7-08df077d13a2&fileId=6bf04f52-04f0-42db-a542-a864f88fd2d0&appItemId=ID21f9957912af47fd8469ee886fb380f5

docs.text:
Agent by itself is good at making decisions and analyzing data. But LLMs naturally can't go and interact with databases and applications... yet. We are going to use tools for that. Tools offer agents both access to critical context from data stored in business applications, and the ability to execute actions based on objectives outlined in the prompt. Tools are how the agent's reasoning and planning can turn into action.

There are various kind of tools we can configure for our agents:

docs.title: Configuring Agent's Prompts
docs.text:
Precision in prompts, like in coding, leads to powerful and predictable results. If your prompt is messy, expect messy output. Treat it like code, and write every word with purpose!

— another advice from gpt-4o

First, let's understand the difference between System prompt and User prompt.

System Prompts provide consistent guidelines that define an agent's role and capabilities, while User Prompts direct its attention to specific tasks and input parameters. Understanding this distinction is essential for effectively designing and implementing AI agents that can perform complex tasks while maintaining appropriate operational boundaries.

  • System prompt — allows you to describe in natural language the agent's role, goal and constraints. You specify any rules for it to follow, and information about when it might want to use certain tools, escalations, or context – all of which we'll cover later in this guide.
  • User prompt — User prompts allow you to structure how the inputs/arguments are passed to the agent, and you can also show in the user prompt how we'll refer to certain inputs in the system prompt.

2. Use the ##Retrieve Income Information## tool to extract the applicant's income information from the existing records.

3. Compare the Paystub income against the extracted income.
- if the paystub income matches exactly with the extracted income, set ##decision## to "valid"
- if there is any discrepancy, set ##decision## to "invalid".

4. If the paystub or existing records data is missing, do not throw an error. Instead, set ##decision## to "invalid".

5. In the ##rationale## field, provide a brief explanation around the decision you've taken.
Maintain confidentiality and handle sensitive information with care.

Output:
{

}

3. Missing/empty/zero data case:

Output:

}

docs.title: Build the Eligibility Determination Agent
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this lesson:

  1. Build a Benefit Eligibility Determination AI Agent from scratch as a coded agent in Python
    • Agent will use the declared applicant's household size and monthly gross income
    • Using benefit claims guidelines and rules, as part of context grounding, it will decide whether the applicant qualifies, what amount they will receive, and a justification
  2. Test the Agent locally, then push it into your solution and debug it in Studio Web
  3. Configure the Agent in the Maestro workflow
  4. Use the output of the Agent when presenting the Benefits Claim case to a human for review

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Implement an agent which decides if the applicant is eligible for benefits and calculates the amount, according to the guidelines. LLMs are ideal for this job, because the guidelines can be in an unstructured format. LLMs can be instructed to treat such scenarios accordingly.

docs.title: General steps for Eligibility & Calculation
docs.text:
This is a two-phase approach to determine benefits: first verifying household eligibility through income thresholds, then calculating the actual benefit amount based on net income and household size.

  1. Income Eligibility Check: Compare the household's gross monthly income against threshold tables based on household size. For example, a single person must have gross income at or below $1,950/month ($23,400/year), while a family of four has a threshold of $4,050/month ($48,600/year). Each additional person adds $700/month to the threshold.
  2. Net Income Calculation: Apply standard deductions to gross income: $198 for households of 1-3 people, $199 for 4 people, $234 for 5 people, and $268 for 6+ people (2025 rates). This yields the household's net monthly income.
  3. Benefit Determination: Use the formula below. Maximum benefits range from $300/month for a single person to $1,785/month for 8-person households, with $225 added per additional person beyond 8.
SNAP Benefit = Maximum Benefit for Household Size - (Net Income × 0.15)

docs.title: Let's build an AI Agent!

Let's use Python to create our Eligibility Determination Agent!

Here is the structure of the agent's inputs and outputs.

docs.title: Low-code vs. coded
docs.text:
In lessons 4 and 5 you built agents in Agent Builder, by filling in forms. A coded agent has the same building blocks, written in Python instead:

Agent Builder (low-code) Coded agent (Python) Input and output arguments Pydantic Input and Output classes Model GPT-5.4, temperature 0 UiPathChat(model="gpt-5.4", temperature=0), routed through the LLM Gateway, no API key System prompt and user prompt SYSTEM_PROMPT and USER_PROMPT_TEMPLATE strings Context Grounding index Eligibility A tool that searches the index with ContextGroundingRetriever Addition, Subtraction and Multiplication tools Three small Python @tool functions The agent loop (think → call tool → answer) create_agent(...), wrapped in a LangGraph StateGraph Debug in Studio Web uip codedagent run locally, then Debug in Studio Web

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Install the prerequisites (skip this if your machine is already set up)

You need three tools: Node.js (for the uip CLI), the uip CLI itself and uv, a fast Python package manager. You don't need to install Python separately: uv downloads the right version in step 2.

Where to run these commands: in a terminal window.

  • Windows: open PowerShell: press the Windows key, type PowerShell and press Enter.
  • Mac: open Terminal: press Cmd + Space, type Terminal and press Enter.

You can run the install commands from any folder. They install the tools for your whole machine, not for one project. After installing a tool, close the terminal and open a new one, so it can find the tool.

For Node.js and uv, check first: if the tool is already installed, update it when needed and move on. Install it only if the check fails with "not recognized" (Windows) or "command not found" (Mac).

1. Node.js

Check:

node --version

npm --version

  • Both print a version: Node.js is installed, don't reinstall it. Just make sure npm is 11.x.x. If it isn't, upgrade it:

    npm install -g npm@11

  • node is not found: install the LTS version:

    WindowsMac 
    winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS

    Download and run the LTS installer from nodejs.org.

    Open a new terminal and run the check again. If npm isn't 11.x.x, upgrade it with the command above.

2. UiPath CLI

No check needed here. This command installs the CLI if it's missing, or updates it to the latest version if you already have it:

npm install -g @uipath/cli@latest

3. uv

Check:

uv --version

  • It prints a version: update it:

    WindowsMac 
    winget upgrade astral-sh.uv

    uv self update

  • uv is not found: install it:

    WindowsMac 
    winget install astral-sh.uv

    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

4. Final check

Open a new terminal, so it finds the newly installed tools, and run:

node --version

npm --version

uip --version

uv --version

Every command prints a version, and npm is 11.x.x.

In the same terminal, go to your Desktop, create an empty folder for the agent and a Python virtual environment inside it. The virtual environment keeps this agent's packages separate from everything else on your machine. It's the coded counterpart of the dependencies Studio Web manages for you.

WindowsMac

mkdir eligibility-determination-coded-agent

cd eligibility-determination-coded-agent

uv venv --python 3.13 --managed-python

--managed-python makes uv download its own Python 3.13 instead of picking whatever is already installed. Coded agents need Python 3.11 to 3.13.

Run the rest of the commands here

From now on, run every command in this folder, with the virtual environment active. Your prompt shows (eligibility-determination-coded-agent). If you open a new terminal, go back into the folder and activate it again:

docs.title: 3. Scaffold the project
docs.text:
Install the UiPath LangGraph integration, point the CLI at your virtual environment and create the project files:

uv pip install uipath-langchain

uip codedagent setup --force

uip codedagent new eligibility-determination-coded-agent

uv sync
  • uipath-langchain brings in the UiPath SDK, LangGraph and LangChain. Installing it first makes uip codedagent new produce a LangGraph template.
  • uip codedagent new creates main.py, langgraph.json and pyproject.toml in the current folder.
  • uv sync installs exactly what pyproject.toml lists and pins the versions in uv.lock, the file Studio Web uses later to install the same versions in the cloud.

Open the folder in your code editor. In pyproject.toml, replace the placeholder author (John Doe) with your own name:

authors = [{ name = "Your Name" }]

docs.title: 4. Start main.py: imports and settings
docs.text:
Delete everything in main.py. Start with the imports and three settings: the model and the Context Grounding index the agent will search.

"""SNAP Eligibility Determination agent (LangGraph)."""

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from uipath_langchain.chat.models import UiPathChat
from uipath_langchain.retrievers import ContextGroundingRetriever

MODEL = "gpt-5.4"
INDEX_NAME = "Eligibility"
INDEX_FOLDER = "Benefit Claims"

Where is the index?

The Eligibility index lives in the Orchestrator folder Benefit Claims. To check it, run:

uip context-grounding list --folder-path "Benefit Claims"

If your trainer gives you a different folder, change INDEX_FOLDER.

docs.title: 5. Define the input and output
docs.text:
Agent arguments let your agent take in information about a business case and return a result, just as you might have activities or processes do. This can allow you to pass information from a trigger in Orchestrator or use the output of an agent to launch another automation.

In a coded agent the arguments are two Python classes, Input and Output. Field(description=...) works like an argument description, and the LLM reads it too. Add them below the settings:

# ---------- Input / Output ----------
class Input(BaseModel):
    Household_Size: int = Field(
        description="The number of people living in the applicant's house"
    )
    Monthly_Gross_Income: str = Field(
        description="The amount of money the applicant's household makes in a month"
    )


class Output(BaseModel):
    Conclusion: bool = Field(
        description="Result of criteria evaluation against provided context"
    )
    Justification: str = Field(
        description="An explanation for the conclusion, or of the inability to verify the criteria."
    )
    Calculation: float | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description="The amount of money the applicant is entitled to per month, if they are determined eligible for benefits.",
    )


class State(Input):
    """Graph state = the input fields plus the output fields filled in by the agent."""

    Conclusion: bool | None = None
    Justification: str | None = None
    Calculation: float | None = None

Fields without a default (Household_Size, Conclusion, Justification) are required. State is what the graph carries around internally: the inputs plus the outputs the agent fills in.

docs.title: Configuring Agent's Prompts
docs.text:
Precision in prompts, like in coding, leads to powerful and predictable results. If your prompt is messy, expect messy output. Treat it like code, and write every word with purpose!

(another advice from gpt-4o)

First, let's understand the difference between System prompt and User prompt.

  • System prompt: describes in natural language the agent's role, goal and constraints: the rules it follows and when to use its tools and context.
  • User prompt: structures how the inputs are passed to the agent, so the system prompt can refer to them.

docs.title: 6. Add the prompts
docs.text:
The System Prompt below ends with one line that tells the model which tool reads the "Eligibility" context. In the User Prompt, {Household_Size} and {Monthly_Gross_Income} are placeholders that Python's .format() fills in with the agent's inputs:

# ---------- Prompts ----------
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """#Role
You are a decision agent whose role is to evaluate if an applicant meets the eligibility criteria for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits. The eligibility criteria is specified in the "Eligibility" context.

#Goals
Assess whether the given applicant information qualifies them for SNAP benefits. Output a conclusion along with an explanation for the decision. For qualified applicants, calculate the monthly benefit amount.

# Instructions
1. Determine the net income. Use the ##SNAP Eligibility## context to do this.
2. Determine if the applicant qualifies for benefits, according to the thresholds from the context.
- Set the Boolean value of ##Conclusion## to True if they qualify, or False if they don't.
3. Set the string value of ##Justification## to your explanation of the eligibility recommendation.
If they qualify for benefits:
 a. Calculate the maximum benefit amount for the household size.
 b. Set the value of ##Calculation## to the final benefit amount.
If they don't qualify for benefits:
 a. Set the value of ##Calculation## to "0".

##Calculation Rules
**DO NOT** make calculations directly, instead use the available tools (**Addition Tool**, **Subtraction Tool**, **Multiplication tool**) to make calculations.

Use the search_eligibility_context tool to read the "Eligibility" context."""

USER_PROMPT_TEMPLATE = (
    "Decide whether this applicant qualifies for SNAP benefits:\n"
    "Household Size: {Household_Size}\n"
    "Monthly Gross Income: {Monthly_Gross_Income}"
)

docs.title: Context Grounding
docs.text:
Context Grounding is a component of the UiPath AI Trust Layer which allows you to bring in your data to generate more accurate, reliable GenAI predictions.

You can create representative indexes and embeddings of business data that UiPath GenAI features can reference for contextual evidence at runtime. An index is a searchable copy of your documents: when the agent asks a question, it gets back the passages that match best.

In this case, we are going to use context grounding to provide the agent with the Benefit Eligibility criteria and calculation rules, to enable it to make the right decisions.

The Eligibility Criteria and Benefit Calculation Rules documents are indexed inside the Eligibility context grounding index.

Benefit Calculation Rules.

Eligibility Criteria.

A coded agent reaches the index through a tool: the LLM decides what to search for, and the tool returns the most relevant passages.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Agent by itself is good at making decisions and analyzing data. But LLMs naturally can't go and interact with databases and applications... yet. We are going to use tools for that. Tools offer agents both access to critical context from data stored in business applications, and the ability to execute actions based on objectives outlined in the prompt. Tools are how the agent's reasoning and planning can turn into action.

docs.title: 7. Add the tools
docs.text:
Four tools: one searches the Eligibility index, and three do the arithmetic the benefit amount needs. The docstring of each tool is the description the LLM reads to decide when to use it.

Why local math tools?

You could give the agent RPA or API workflows as tools for the arithmetic. We are going to use Python functions instead, because they run inside the agent: they're faster, and they don't start an Orchestrator job for every calculation. The prompt rule "DO NOT make calculations directly" stays, so the LLM still has to use a tool for every step.

# ---------- Tools ----------
@tool
async def search_eligibility_context(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the "Eligibility" context (SNAP eligibility rules: deductions,
    income thresholds and maximum benefit amounts by household size).

    Args:
        query: Natural-language question about the SNAP eligibility rules.
    """
    retriever = ContextGroundingRetriever(
        index_name=INDEX_NAME,
        folder_path=INDEX_FOLDER,
        number_of_results=3,
    )
    documents = await retriever.ainvoke(query)
    return "\n\n".join(doc.page_content for doc in documents)


@tool
def addition_tool(FirstValue: float, SecondValue: float) -> dict:
    """Addition Tool: adds two numbers and returns FirstValue + SecondValue."""
    return {"AdditionResult": FirstValue + SecondValue}


@tool
def subtraction_tool(FirstValue: float, SecondValue: float) -> dict:
    """Subtraction Tool: subtracts two numbers and returns FirstValue - SecondValue."""
    return {"SubtractionResult": FirstValue - SecondValue}


@tool
def multiplication_tool(FirstValue: float, SecondValue: float) -> dict:
    """Multiplication tool: multiplies two numbers and returns FirstValue * SecondValue."""
    return {"MultiplicationResult": FirstValue * SecondValue}


TOOLS = [search_eligibility_context, addition_tool, subtraction_tool, multiplication_tool]
  • number_of_results=3 returns the three most relevant passages. The default would be 10.

docs.title: 8. Build the agent and the graph
docs.text:
create_agent runs the familiar loop: the LLM reads the prompt, calls tools, reads the results and repeats until it can answer. response_format=Output makes it return a validated Output object.

# ---------- Agent ----------
async def determine_eligibility(state: State) -> dict:
    # The LLM and the ReAct agent are created inside the node (never at import time).
    llm = UiPathChat(model=MODEL, temperature=0)
    agent = create_agent(
        model=llm,
        tools=TOOLS,
        system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
        response_format=Output,
    )
    user_prompt = USER_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(
        Household_Size=state.Household_Size,
        Monthly_Gross_Income=state.Monthly_Gross_Income,
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [HumanMessage(content=user_prompt)]},
        config={"recursion_limit": 50},  # up to 25 agent iterations
    )
    output: Output = result["structured_response"]
    return output.model_dump()

The graph wraps the agent in a single step and tells UiPath what the inputs and outputs are:

# ---------- Graph ----------
builder = StateGraph(State, input_schema=Input, output_schema=Output)
builder.add_node("determine_eligibility", determine_eligibility)
builder.add_edge(START, "determine_eligibility")
builder.add_edge("determine_eligibility", END)

graph = builder.compile()

Create the LLM inside the function

UiPathChat(...) needs your UiPath login. Creating it at the top of the file would try to authenticate as soon as the file is imported, and the next step would fail.

# ---------- Input / Output ----------
class Input(BaseModel):

    )

    )

    )
    Calculation: float | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description="The amount of money the applicant is entitled to per month, if they are determined eligible for benefits.",

class State(Input):
    """Graph state = the input fields plus the output fields filled in by the agent."""

    Conclusion: bool | None = None
    Justification: str | None = None
    Calculation: float | None = None


# ---------- Prompts ----------
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """#Role
You are a decision agent whose role is to evaluate if an applicant meets the eligibility criteria for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits. The eligibility criteria is specified in the "Eligibility" context.

#Goals
Assess whether the given applicant information qualifies them for SNAP benefits. Output a conclusion along with an explanation for the decision. For qualified applicants, calculate the monthly benefit amount.

# Instructions
1. Determine the net income. Use the ##SNAP Eligibility## context to do this.
2. Determine if the applicant qualifies for benefits, according to the thresholds from the context.
- Set the Boolean value of ##Conclusion## to True if they qualify, or False if they don't.
3. Set the string value of ##Justification## to your explanation of the eligibility recommendation.
If they qualify for benefits:
 a. Calculate the maximum benefit amount for the household size.
 b. Set the value of ##Calculation## to the final benefit amount.
If they don't qualify for benefits:
 a. Set the value of ##Calculation## to "0".

##Calculation Rules
**DO NOT** make calculations directly, instead use the available tools (**Addition Tool**, **Subtraction Tool**, **Multiplication tool**) to make calculations.

Use the search_eligibility_context tool to read the "Eligibility" context."""

USER_PROMPT_TEMPLATE = (
    "Decide whether this applicant qualifies for SNAP benefits:\n"
    "Household Size: {Household_Size}\n"
    "Monthly Gross Income: {Monthly_Gross_Income}"
)


# ---------- Tools ----------
@tool
async def search_eligibility_context(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the "Eligibility" context (SNAP eligibility rules: deductions,
    income thresholds and maximum benefit amounts by household size).

    Args:
        query: Natural-language question about the SNAP eligibility rules.
    """
    retriever = ContextGroundingRetriever(
        index_name=INDEX_NAME,
        folder_path=INDEX_FOLDER,
        number_of_results=3,
    )
    documents = await retriever.ainvoke(query)
    return "\n\n".join(doc.page_content for doc in documents)


@tool
def addition_tool(FirstValue: float, SecondValue: float) -> dict:
    """Addition Tool: adds two numbers and returns FirstValue + SecondValue."""
    return {"AdditionResult": FirstValue + SecondValue}


@tool
def subtraction_tool(FirstValue: float, SecondValue: float) -> dict:
    """Subtraction Tool: subtracts two numbers and returns FirstValue - SecondValue."""
    return {"SubtractionResult": FirstValue - SecondValue}


@tool
def multiplication_tool(FirstValue: float, SecondValue: float) -> dict:
    """Multiplication tool: multiplies two numbers and returns FirstValue * SecondValue."""
    return {"MultiplicationResult": FirstValue * SecondValue}


TOOLS = [search_eligibility_context, addition_tool, subtraction_tool, multiplication_tool]


# ---------- Agent ----------
async def determine_eligibility(state: State) -> dict:
    # The LLM and the ReAct agent are created inside the node (never at import time).
    llm = UiPathChat(model=MODEL, temperature=0)
    agent = create_agent(
        model=llm,
        tools=TOOLS,
        system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
        response_format=Output,
    )
    user_prompt = USER_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(
        Household_Size=state.Household_Size,
        Monthly_Gross_Income=state.Monthly_Gross_Income,
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [HumanMessage(content=user_prompt)]},
        config={"recursion_limit": 50},  # up to 25 agent iterations
    )
    output: Output = result["structured_response"]
    return output.model_dump()


# ---------- Graph ----------
builder = StateGraph(State, input_schema=Input, output_schema=Output)
builder.add_node("determine_eligibility", determine_eligibility)
builder.add_edge(START, "determine_eligibility")
builder.add_edge("determine_eligibility", END)

graph = builder.compile()

docs.text:
Time to test it by giving it some sample inputs. Usually you will need to come back multiple times and improve the prompt in order for it to be more flexible. This way users need to perform less manual validations and it will work more reliably.

Each command passes the input straight to the agent. The result appears in the terminal when the run finishes: Conclusion, Justification and Calculation, followed by ✓ Successful execution.

Qualifies: household of 4Does not qualify: household of 1 WindowsMac 
uip codedagent run agent '{\"Household_Size\": 4, \"Monthly_Gross_Income\": \"2500\"}'

uip codedagent run agent '{"Household_Size": 4, "Monthly_Gross_Income": "2500"}'

According to the guidelines, the applicant qualifies, because the maximum allowed gross income for a household of 4 is $4,050.

Output should be Conclusion: true, Calculation: 649.85

WindowsMac 
uip codedagent run agent '{\"Household_Size\": 1, \"Monthly_Gross_Income\": \"2000\"}'

uip codedagent run agent '{"Household_Size": 1, "Monthly_Gross_Income": "2000"}'

According to the guidelines, the applicant does not qualify, because the maximum allowed gross income for a household of 1 is $1,950, which the applicant's income exceeds.

  • agent is the entry-point name from langgraph.json, not the project name.
  • Add --output-file result.json if you also want to save the result as a JSON file.
  • Add --trace-file trace.jsonl to save every LLM and tool call. For the household of 4 you'll see one search of the index, then subtraction_tool(2500, 199), multiplication_tool(2301, 0.15) and subtraction_tool(995, 345.15). The tools did the maths, not the LLM.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 drops the double quotes inside a JSON argument, so each " is written as \". In PowerShell 7.3 or newer, use the Mac form instead. Check your version with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion.

UiPath Integration Service is the fastest and most convenient way to automate API enabled applications. It takes care of authorization and authentication, helping you centralize management of API connections and also allowing faster integration into SaaS platforms.

  • Provides curated activities and events (with additional data filters) for ease of use.
  • Simplifies automation design by providing a uniform experience across all Studio designers.

A connection is an authenticated link to one application account, for example one Gmail mailbox. Your automations use the connection to call that application, so nobody has to type credentials into a workflow.

docs.title: 1. See what's available
